House in Committee on Bill No. 10, to amend the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Act; Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-section 5 of the Act repealed ; and new section 5 substituted- Power to make regulations:

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
There is one clause in the Bill as it came down from the committee that should be struck out. That is subsection 3 of new section 5, reading as follows:
In the event of the appropriation made for this work for the fiscal year 1919-20 not being sufficient for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act, the Governor in Council may order that any further moneys required, not exceeding in the aggregate the sum of fifteen mi'lion dollars, shall be paid out of the appropriation for demobilization purposes.
Since the committee made its report, estimates have been brought down to the House providing for a sum of $40,000,000 for

whatever expenditures are required to carry out the recommendations of the committee. Consequently, this clause is not necessary. I would therefore move that subsection 3 of section 5 be struck from the Bill.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: Do I understand that this should be moved before we consider clause 5a?

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
No; we can do it when
we come to subsection 3.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to get some information on this subject.. The report, at page 53, says this:
Regarding their proposals generally, apart from the financial considerations involved, your committee cannot see their way clear to recommend any form of financial assistance for any particular class or group of ex-members of the forces who were not disabled. Your committee are convinced that the great majority of the men themselves would be the first to resent any such distinction.
I skip over to page 54, second paragraph, which goes on as follows:
While the special claims of university students were pressed in the strongest possible way, your committee, after the fullest consideration of the problem' as a whole, finally reached the conclusion that the State could not justly and equitably provide for them without making equal provision for the mechanic, the fisherman, the miner, the business man, the industrial worker, and all others who through war service suffered serious loss or hardship in reference to their training, occupation, business, property, equipment, or homes.
This afternoon I, as a supporter of the amendment, agreed tacitly to its withdrawal on the undertaking of this House that in the event of representations being made to the .Government affecting any number of men who might constitute a class the Government would entertain these representations and hear those who were making the same. I do not believe that the undertaking was in exactly the same verbiage as I am using at the present time but the statement which I have made is substantially the same thing. Now, the Bill says this:
The minister shall have the management and control of all such matters as are assigned to him from time to time by the Governor In Council, relating in any way to the re-establishment in civil life of all persons who, since August 1, 1914, served in the Naval or Military Forces of His Majesty or any of His Majesty's Allies, and to the care of the dependents of such persons.
The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) presented an amendment ' which was covered by the declaration made in this House by the minister himself and I feel, like all others, that we should have confidence in our ministers, until such
time as we are absolutely convinced that their word of honour in the House of Parliament means nothing. To give consideration to what will be needed to re-establish in civil life of all returned soldiers is going to involve a great deal of work and time, and the minister in control of these matters is going to be overtaxed. If it is true that certain representations are to be made, we will say, by the mechanics, all over the Dominion, by the medical students, and by the law students-because the Government has decided not to enter into the general proposition of granting	gratuitiesit is utterly impossible for the minister to give consideration to every one of the representations that may be made to him. Therefore, I have an amendment to suggest. I would like this clause to be amended in such a way as to make provision for the appointment of a commission consisting of returned soldiers, members of Parliament, and a member of the Government, to receive and hear all these various complaints which may be made, to determine as to the necessity which exists in each and every case, and to provide for cases that may be passed upon as necessitous or actually deserving of consideration. I submit if the minister in charge of the department is to make that department a success he has already sufficient duties that require his best attention. If he should also be called upon to meet the wants and needs of the various people throughout the Dominion who may wish to present their several cases, his task will be rendered altogether too great. The report of the Special Committee gives, under the title of "Vocational Training," an illustration of the large number of classes who may apply. Is the minister going to be the sole person interested in this matter? I take it from the observations that were made here this afternoon that the Government will be held responsible, and that all sorts of recommendations and suggestions may be made to them to be adopted or rejected, as the case may be. Furthermore, I gather the impression from the statement made by the minister (Air. Calder) this afternoon that it was the intention of the Government to consider every scheme that may be submitted.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: Stick to the question.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman and his friends would not interrupt malapropos I would adhere to the question; but inasmuch as they choose to interject matter which is not relevant to the question

I feel that I am not bound to be a target for them.
I submit frankly and candidly that the Bill should be amended in such a way as to afford the proper redress to the men in this 'Country who are affected. As the clause now stands it is entirely too limited in its scope to secure that consideration which should be given to the men as a whole throughout the Dominion. Therefore, I move to add the following -as subclause (2):
2. The Governor in Council shall appoint a commission consisting' of two members of Parliament, two returned soldiers and a minister of the Crown for the purpose of making a thorough investigation of the returned soldiers' needs and devising a plan whereunder all the soldiers who have taken part in the war would be given all the assistance they may require.
Amendment (Mr. Mackie) negatived.

Section agreed to.
On paragraph (b)-Minister authorized to engage technical and special temporary staff, notwithstanding Civil Service Act:

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
This paragraph
certainly requires an explanation. We have passed amendments to the Civil Service Act requiring that appointments to the public service shall be made by the Commission, and here we are deliberately proposing to set that law aside. There may be good reasons for doing this-I know the matter is referred to in the Committee's report'-but I should like to have an explanation as to why the Civil Service Act is to be ignored in this instance -and not in the ease of the other departments.
Mr. iOALDER:	In reference to this proposed amendment, which was not in the Bill as origin-ally introduced, after we had taken evidence, and during the course of that evidence, every member of the Committee was impressed, I think, with the necessity of enabling this department to get its expert and technical staff just as
quickly as	it -could	get	it.	Underthe ordinary routine	in	the	CivilService it	takes, we	will	say,	froma month	to six weeeks,	and	sometimes more, to have an appointment made. At the present time, as was explained by an hon. member this afternoon, this work is increasing very rapidly, peak loads, it is expected, will be reached sometime in February, and some of the men employed in this department-and there is a very large number of them-knowing that sections of the work will cease within a year or two, whenever they get an opportunity for per-
manent employment in the outside world take advantage of it. As a consequence the department feels that it should be placed in a position to get this technical expert staff quickly. There is another factor, and a very important one, which came out repeatedly in the evidence. It was represented, and,
I think, -correctly, that, in addition to the work being largely of a temporary character -that is, these men are not appointed per-mently, for large sections of this work will cease in a year or two-there is an element in the work of this department that does not appear in the work of other departments, the human element. The department has to take into consideration the character of these experts, their attitude towards the work, and whether or not they will be sympathetic in their relationship with the returned men, because these experts are dealing with men who require special care and treatment. For that rason the department is anxious that.it shall be allowed to take into consideration, not only the ability of a man to pass certain examinations, that is only one feature of it, but also the question whether he posseses those traits of character which -are necessary in order to carry on this work successfully. Therefore the department wishes to be in a position either to promote suitable men already in the service, or to be able to get men of the right type just as soon as possible, more especially because the work has been increasing very rapidly and the conditions are such that there should not be any delay. You cannot delay where you are dealing with disabled men, you cannot afford to take time to look around and choose men in the ordinary way as in the other departments of the service. That was the viewpoint presented to our committee, and after fully discussing the matter every member of the committee came to the conclusion that this exception should he made in so far as this department is concerned, particularly in view of the fact that as regards a large number of these appointments they will not be permanent. Let me illustrate.
If I remenber the figures, there are now about 13,000 men undergoing vocational training. The average length of the course is eight months, -and as soon as those men complete their training it is estimated that another batch of 8,000 or 10,000 men will succeed them to go through the same course. But when that training is completed the experts remain no longer in the public [DOT] service. So that this department in that respect is not on all fours with the other departments of the service, and I think the

recommendation here is one that will commend itself to the good judgment of the House.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: What other classes of technical service are contemplated by this section? For instance, medical service is technical.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: Yes. I think that would be included.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
The Civil Service Act
has its disadvantages, one of which is delay, and delay is no more agreeable in other departments than it is in the department in which my hon. friend presides. I tried to live loyally up to the Civil Service Act, but one of the misfortunes of working under it is the long time it takes to do anything, so that people become impatient. The departments try to get over that by making temporary appointments, and although it is embarrassing, it results in the Civil Service Commission eventually making the appointments. This does not contemplate temporary appointments to be confirmed later by the Civil Service Commission. Although the hon. gentleman tells us they are not meant to be permanent employees, I,am inclined to think that under the wording of the section they would be. Our experience has been that wherever any loophole is left efforts will be made to push some person into the Civil Service. What my hon. friend says about the need of appointments being made promptly would be said by the minister of any other department, and I am a little afraid that after all our boasting about the Civil Service Act, our boasting that a member of Parliament above every one else in the world must not have anything to do with appointments, the ministers are trying to hav* something to do with them in this particular matter.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
I think in so far as the department itself and the Government are concerned, if the committee considers it advisable that the appointment of these officers should be left in the ordinary course to the Civil Service Commission, it will accept that view. But after hearing all the evidence and arguments, insofar as this department is concerned, personally I am convinced, and I think I voice the opinion of every member of the committee on both sides of the House, that where you have a department dealing with disabled men, with men who are sick, you cannot afford to have delay in appointing technical experts to take care of them. When those sick men need attention they must get it, and
the work cannot be blocked, there must not be any cessation of it. What the hon. gentleman says with reference to the necessity of having appointments made in the other departments is true; but all these appointments are practically temporary, and the wording of the section itself indicates that. Paragraph (b), subsection 2, new section 5, provides for the employment "of such technical and special temporary staff"-not permanent staff. These men are all regarded as being [DOT] taken on temporarily, because large sections of this work will not continue beyond a certain period.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: Temporary service may mean quite a period.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: Yes, twelve or eighteen months.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: In any other department you could not make an appointment of that character without the Civil Service Commission intervening. In all departments where there is urgency I would give the minister power to make a temporary appointment, but with the condition that the Civil Service Commission should get busy immediately and the appointment should be confirmed in the regular way. There is nothing in which we are more likely to get into trouble after passing the Civil Service Act than by making loopholes in this form or in the form of a vote in the Estimates whereby men may be appointed without complying with the Civil Service conditions.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: I quite agree in a general way with what my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) has said. But my experience in regard to appointments for soldiers' civil reestablishment is that we are only looking to young surgeons and vocational officers who do not intend to take up the Civil Service as a profession. It is really war work continued, and the delay in making appointments which must occur under the Civil Service Act would be almost fatal to the director of the department getting the best men quickly and making special arrangements with them so that they could remain for a certain time.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: How long?

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
I do not know. But some of them would be willing to stay away from their professions for six months, special arrangements being made with them. You could not do that through the Civil Service Commission. The Civil Service Com-

mission has a great deal to do at the present time in licking the Act into shape and making it workable, and it seems to me it would be far better if the minister would stick to the Bill and not, as I understood him, accept any suggestion that these appointments should come under the Civil Service Commission. We all know the sacrifices that have been made by the medical profession, by expert instructors and mechanics in the other branches,of vocational training, in order to carry on this patriotic work. I should not think it wise to bring these officers under the technical and rigid rules of the Civil Service Commission in the matter of appointments. They are here one month and there the next; being professional men, they can do their work under a temporary tenure. I think it would be far better to let the clause stand as it is.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
I hope
the minister will allow the clause to stand as it is. The first thing to be regarded here is efficiency. The Civil Service Commission cannot be a judge of everything, much less can it be a judge in the matter of the appointment of scientific men and of officers to carry on this work of technical education. I am strongly of opinion that to get the best men you must put the responsibility upon the head of the department and give him the power to build up a staff which will be efficient. The whole thing comes back, as I have said on previous occasions in the House, to the impossibility of having three- men run the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific; of having three men be the final authority and judgment upon everything. The thing is absurd, it is preposterous; and I do not think the country will stand for it.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
I admit the difliculty
in the matter, but any argument my hon. Friend (Mr. McGibbon) has used would apply also to the employment of technical officers in any other branch of the service; yet in every other branch of the service the Civil Service Act must be complied with.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: I would extend the same principle to all.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: That is another question.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
In certain cases a departure has been made from the rule or regulation that the Civil Service Commission shall make all appointments. For-instance, when experts were required by

the Finance Department in connection with the Victory Loans and the income tax, work not of a 'permanent character, the appointees were selected not by the Civil Service Commission, but through the head of the department, the Minister of Finance. The same thing has' been done before in the case' of work of a temporary nature, for just the reason that is stated here.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: For another reason I think that we should stick to the recommendation 'that has been made by the Committee. If we g,a back to the Civil Service Act, delay will be involved in the appointments, and that will necessarily result in delay to the returned soldiers themselves. If there is one thing that has irritated and annoyed returned men in connection with the work of this department it is the numerous delays which have occurred, delays which were unavoidable simply because the necessary technical assistance could not be properly obtained to put into working order the particular branch of the department in question. If we add to that delay we shall .simply add to the irritation of these men. I want to see that source of irritation removed, consequently I want to see these appointments made as quickly as possible so that the work may be carried out promptly and efficiently.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: It is another form of repealing the Civil Service Act.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
Can it not be said that the whole staff of the department is, in a sense, temporary? Another thing: although I have read this report with considerable care I do not find that the committee went into the question of the administration of the department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment. I have heard that there is considerable abuse in that department in the matter of moving the soildiers from place to place. I cannot give the details, but that has been suggested to me from different quarters. If, then, the whole staff is temporary, why not say frankly that the technical staff shall he appointed by the minister?
Mr. MeKENZIE:	What is meant by
"technical and special officers"?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
The officials of the department are employed temporarily, because the department itself is a temporary one. The vocational training staff are employed on the understanding that they may be retired on a month's notice. Applications for vocational training must all

be in by February 1 of next year. Courses commencing on that date will Last from seven to ten months, so that by the end of next year the department itself will go out of business so far as vocational training is concerned. Suppose a man is required as an instructor in the vocational school at Vancouver. If the usual procedure is had through the Civil Service Commission, weeks and months elapse before an appointment can be made. I quoted figures this afternoon to show that over four thousand extra men came in during the last month to take vocational training. As the member for Regina (Mr. Cowan) said, it is necessary that these appointments be made promptly. Returned soldiers, particularly disabled soldiers, are naturally impatient, and if there is delay we are apt to get into considerable trouble.
Mr. MoMASTER: Is there not in the Civil Service Act a provision for temporary employment by ministers?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: I think there is.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
Why does that not meet
the case, then?

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: There is a provision in respect of temporary employees, but it covers only cases of employment for a short period.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: My hon. friend has not answered my question. Vocational training covers .a great variety of subjects. The training of men to be carpenters, shoemakers, automobile mechanics, and followers of many other trades is called "vocational training," but you would not call the instructors in some of these trades technical men. I do not want to disparage any trade, but I never heard of a shoemaker being called a technical man; he would not come under the high-sounding designation of a man who would get into the service under the old section 21, which was so famous in the history of the Civil Service. What I was asking was: Who gets in under this phrase "technical and special?"

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: The Government is empowered under the recomendations of the committee to take all necessary steps to deal with what we call "problem cases." Neurological experts will be required, medical experts and psychiatrists will be required. These would come under the head, I take it, of technical men.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
I quite see the point of the leader of the Opposition. The term "technical and special expert" would not apply
to the clerical staff. Vocational training is divided into two branches, as it were. The men are first trained in educational institutions, and in connection with that work there must be instructors.
In our technical schools, for example, which the ordinary high-school boy attends, there are instructors in carpentry, blacksmithing, and so on, and they are all experts in the trade they are teaching. That is one side of the work. After the men have taken a few weeks or months instruction in some trade, during which time they are gaining a knowledge of its underlying principles, they pass out into the industrial world and go into the shops. There are no instructors there except their fellow-workers. I think the term would apply to all instructors used -by the department in connection with the educational side of their work. It would also apply, I would think, to the men classed as inspectors, follow-up men, and industrial survey men. In Toronto or Montreal, for instance, the department has a number of men who are constantly going over the different industries for the purpose of finding opportunities for employment. This fitting in of the proper man for the job is a very interesting and very delicate piece of work, and requires, perhaps I should not say a technical man, but certainly one of considerable experience and' with a knowledge of human nature. Then, as regards the medical institutions, hospitals and sanitoria of different kinds, practically every man employed outside of the clerical staff might very well be regarded as a technical man in the sense in which that word is used in the Bill.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: There is another feature on which I should like enlightenment. In connection with the hospitals there is a medical service and there is a dental service, and a great many of the medical men and dentists work only part time with the Government, attending to their practice in the other part of the day. Would it be possible under the Civil Service Act to take these men into the Government service if they are only giving part time to the Government? I do not think there is any clause in the Act which would enable us to do that.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: As I understand the minister's answer, every single person the department requires could come in without any examination.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: Oh, no; the clerical staff could not, for instance, and it is an enormous staff.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: Take the case of a man who is working in a store and has a sufficient knowledge of book-keeping to act as an instructor. Suppose, besides acting as a salesman in the store, he undertakes to teach single entry book-keeping to a man taking vocational training, would not he at once become a technical man? I think he could be hired under this provision. Or suppose a man is going to try an examination for mining engineer or mine manager and requires coaching in mathematics. We will suppose that a man in a certain store is a good mathematician, and besides doing his ordinary work around the store takes a soldier under his wing under the advice of the department, to coach him in mathematics for the examination. The moment he becomes an instructor in mathematics he will be a technical man under this section. So the section has the widest possible seope. Certainly a doctor or a lawyer or the highest class of engineer would be considered technical men, and under this section you could go down the list and include almost any kind of worker; a blacksmith, for instance, who undertakes to teach a man horseshoeing, which I regard as one of the highest arts in life, could be included under this provision. I do not see where you are going to stop, and we might as well say that anybody can be employed by this department notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act. It has that wide scope whether the minister intends it or not.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
In the Canada Gazette we have some examples of how the technical service is dealt with in other departments. Here are some men who are wanted and who are required to make application to the Civil Service Commision and comply with the Civil Service Act: an Instructor in Physics, salary $1,000 per annum; an assistant to the Dominion Poultry Husbandman, Department of Agriculture, salary $1,800-that is certainly a technical position; Plant Pathologist, Department of Agriculture, salary $2,160; a District Seed Inspector, Department of Agriculture,-also a technical position; Assistant to Superintendent, Experimental Farm at Ros-thern, $1,320; Assistant to Superintendent of Experimental Farm at Charlottown; Assistant to Superintendent Experimental Farm, at Kapuskasing. These are all technical officers for the various departments, and they all have to go through the Civil Service mill. But if any one desires to appoint a friend to a position in the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment 
Department he does not have to comply with the Civil Service regulations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: In the cases mentioned by the hon. gentleman there does not exist the same necessity for haste in the appointments.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: The persons referred to by the hon. gentleman in his citation from the Canada Gazette are men who are making up their minds to enter upon a Civil Service career. They take a small initial salary, with a maximum in view. I gather from my hon. friend's remarks that he is of the opinion that patronage will play a part in the work of the Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. He must see, however, that this is a special department and there is no opportunity for patronage. The department has to go out and persuade surgeons to come in and help for a short period, which i3 the reverse of patronage. You could not get these gentlemen to come in at small salaries. They must be paid at the proper rate for professional services. They are all looking forward to professional careers and any time they spend in the department will be simply time given to the department and the country, as it were war work in a special service. In addition to that, it is almost certain that nearly all of them will be returned men who have acquired experience at the front. The idea of patronage does not therefore enter into the matter.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has
not as large an experience as I have in the appointment of officials. From my observation, it is ordinarily an easy matter to get a man into the public service-at any rate, it will be so in this department-but it is not so easy to get him out again, no matter in what branch he may be.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext:
What the hon. gentleman says is quite true. It is one of the curses of the Civil Service that once a man gets in he is there for life. At least everyone thinks he is. I want to emphasize one important feature, and that is the human element. We must have had before us in the neighbourhood of fifteen or twenty of the officers in charge of this work, and one thing that struck us forcibly in our inquiry was the type of man that is doing that work. Their character was apparent in the evidence they gave before the Committee. Their mentality and their relationships with their comrades fit them especially for their work. How in the world is the Civil Service Commission, by any method it may employ, going to be able to secure the type

of man that is wanted? That can be done only by those directly connected with the work and possessing the necessary qualifications in order to carry on the department. It is not like putting men in the Finance Department or the Department of Immigration and Colonization. The Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is dealing with the human element, and it is most essential that when they require men there should be no delay in getting them. It is also highly important that the right type of men with the proper qualities should be selected. It was largely for that reason that the Committee favourably viewed the suggestion that the selection of these men should be left with those who are directly connected with the work. Personally, I am firmly of the opinion that that should be done.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: If any latitude is necessary to obtain speedy appointments it should be given to the Civil Service Commission, who are in touch with the whole of Canada, and know where officials are obtainable. They have long lists of men who have passed civil service examinations, and they are certainly more in touch with the country at large than any single department could be. If a technical man were required in this department the Civil Service Commission could obtain him as speedily as the department could, and there would still be centralization in the matter of appointments. I do not think you should spread this power of appointment all over creation. There is some responsibility on the shoulders of the Civil Service Commission, and they are sensible of it. I repeat that that Commission should secure these men instead of leaving this work to the hundred and one departments that we have. If a deputy minister wants a man he telephones to the Commission and they can secure him much more expeditiously than can any individual in a department.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: Suppose a man were required at short notice for some particular work in Vancouver, what would be the procedure of the Civil Service Commission to obtain him? Would they not have to advertise or have some one acquafinated with the place make inquiries in order to obtain that man? In my opinion it would be an easier matter for this department to get the 'man they needed than to leave that work to the Civil Service Commission.

maintopic: VISIT OF THE PRINCE OF WALES.
speechtext: I may mention something that came under my observation the

other day in regard to that very province. In some department in British Columbia a man was required and they wired to the chairman of the Commission who looked up his list. I had a conversation with the head of the department himself; I had nothing to do with the appointment. The chairman of the Commission looked up his list, and found the very man that was required, and immediately wired back. The man had passed an examination and was qualified to take the place and he was immediately appointed. A department would not have any information as to who had passed examinations. If the appointment is left to the deputy minister in any department he will not know who have and who have not passed the necessary examinations, and he may take any man whom he thinks fit. Some other man may have passed the examination after long preparation, and might feel a cause for grievance if he were not given an opportunity of appointment. I repeat that the Commission, having a wider knowledge of the country and knowing those who are qualified, is best fitted to find employees, and can do so as quickly as can a department, if not more quickly.

The hon. gentleman suggests that the Civil Service Commission with its lists can select the men. Does he suggest that the men who are on the lists are going to remain incessantly out of employment until they are employed by the Civil Service Commission? I think it is hardly likely.

I am not saying so,
but there are many cases in which men may be otherwise employed in the meantime. A man may be working in a store; he has passed the examination for a higher position; he is not waiting but he is ready. He is working at something else. When the time comes, he is qualified and when he is called he steps in. He is not idling about the street.

I would like to draw the attention of the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) to an aspect of the case which perhaps he is not aware of. Last summer I saw two carloads of men-lunatics and men who had been shell shocked-being taken to an institution. They were in charge of some six or eight men from this department. One of these lunatics insisted, whenever he moved at all, on riding on the back of one of these attendants. I observed that every time he wanted to move anywhere for any useful purpose or for no purpose at all, this attendant was called up;

he came, the man got on his back and he carried him around. These attendants were supplied by this department by reason of the powers which they have, or have had. or have exercised, of selecting on the spot the men that are required for a particular job. I cannot understand how the Civil Service Commission could, upon short notice, supply half a dozen men for positions of that sort. The department has men in its employ and is constantly training men for this service. It is desired to give employment to men who are trained, men who have sympathy and understanding, and I think it would be a very great mistake if the hands of the department were tied so that they could not immediately avail themselves of the services of such men as they required for that particular work which calls for the exercise of that sympathy and understanding which exists between soldiers who have served together and are usually to be found in the immediate neighbourhood of these institutions.

Does the hon. gentleman say that a man of this class would be a technical man?
Mr. GRIEiSBACH: He would be special, he would be temporary, and he might even be technical if he developed himself along those lines.

The problem that is
before us is apparently not unsolvable. Hard cases make bad law, and where you find a difficult case the tendency is away from good law. I can understand the desire of the minister not to hamper the men who are in charge of a hospital. A doctor in charge of a hospital for subnormal cases wishes to have the power to pick his own staff. There may be practising in the neighbourhood some young doctor of sympathetic mind and heart who has made a study of insanity or subnormal cases. The man in charge of the hospital would like to get such a man as that and, of course, would like to have more or less of a free hand in the choice of such a man. I think it is desirable that that should be allowed in the selection of the technical members of the staff. Neither the minister nor the deputy can make the choice personally. This choice that is confided to the minister under the Bill will be exercised at perhaps a score of different places throughout Canada. How would it do, in order to prevent abuse, to give the right of appointment subject to confirmation within a certain time by the Civil Service Commission? There is a great deal to be said for giving

the person in'charge of a department a free hand, but against that the people in their wisdom have come to the conclusion that there (should be a controlling force, and that force the Civil Service Commission. My suggestion would be that, if the power under the Civil Service Act to make a temporary appointment is not wide enough to cover .such a case as I have spoken about, wider power might be taken by the minister, but it should always be subject to confirmation by the Civil Service Commission within a reasonable time.
How long a time?

I would say perhaps
nine months. I think that under the ordinary law the minister has six months. That is not sufficient and I would give a longer time. But if the minister is allowed to have a free hand in connection with this department it will constitute an exceedingly unwholesome precedent if other ministers come forward and ask the same power in connection with their departments. There should be some control of a power of this sort, that is as far as technical men are concerned. As far as the special temporary staff is concerned, I think the case I have made out in regard to technical assistants is still stronger here. If it is necessary to have a special temporary staff-and I can quite understand that when you are dealing with sick people you cannot wait-The minister must have the power, (I think the minister now has the power under the Civil Service Act) to obtain what he requires immediately. I would not have these people appointed without reference sooner or later to the Civil Service Commission, in order to prevent the creeping in of abuses. Let me give an instance. In the part of the country I have the honour to represent there has been a farm offered for sale for years for $2,200. Recently the department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment bought that farm for $4,000 and some poor, unfortunate soldier is being put upon it and is undertaking to pay back in a term of years the price of $4,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is the Land Settlement Board.
The Land Settlement Board. I do not know whether the minister responsible for the Land Settlement Board is here or not.	.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No.

Well then the minister, will bring this striking instance to his attention in order that he may have an opportunity of correcting this fault, because it is a fault. Land is being purchased at far more than its market value and men being put on this land with an obligation to ,pay for it within a term of years; but the fact that it has been purchased at far more than its market value is something that, I fear, will make it impossible. I suppose the man who valued that farm for the Board did not make a proper valuation. These are the reasons why I would urge the minister to consider the inadvisability of getting away altogether from the Civil Service Commission.

Personally I am inclined to accept the suggestion of the hon. gentleman (Mr. McMaster). As a matter of fact the committee had that in mind when they inserted in the Act that this authority was to be given to the minister subject to rules and regulations to be approved by the Governor in Council. The committee had it in mind that the rules and the regulations would call for the eventual ratification by the Civil Service Commission. If the committee think that the clause itself should set that forth clearly we can amend it in that respect. One of the members of the committee has called to my mind the discussion that we had. We clearly had in mind at the time the idea that this power should not be exercised except under rules to be made by the Governor in 'Council and that these rules should embody the idea that the commissio'n should finally approve of them.
It does not say so because it distinctly declares that you shall not be interfered with under the Civil Service Act.

If the committee agree
with the idea, we will have an amendment prepared and the clause modified. Probably if we have that understanding and we get through with the rest of the Bill this evening, we might let it go and have the amendment made in the Senate because, they are anxious that we should get through with the Bill so that it could go to the Senate in the morning.

The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) asked how in the event of an appointment being made in British Columbia the Civil Service Commission could act. May I ask how the minister would propose to act 120J '
under this clause in a case of that sort? How would he make an appointment in British Columbia?

In Vancouver they have certain technical officers now on the job probably handling about 1,500 men in that city. They have the best officers that can be got for that work. I think that, beyond question, when a vacancy occurs the minister would give the district vocational officer full power to select a qualified man for that vacancy. He makes the selection on the spot and forwards the recommendation to Ottawa.
Mr. MACKENZIE KlTNG: Would the minister think of communicating with the member for the constituency before making the appointment?
In connection with this work? I do not think so.
I would like to make sure on that point. As I read the clause it seems to leave the door open to that possibility.

The evidence that was given to us, and I think it is correct, is that the department has the greatest difficulty in getting men and holding them, because the work is looked upon as temporary; there is no future in connection with it. There is, therefore, not very much opportunity for what you might call political patronage in connection with the work of the department. Furthermore, the great majority of the men in the employ of the department are returned men. Even the technical officers are practically all returned men and many of them are making very considerable sacrifices to stay with this work. I have spoken to them, and one told me he would like to get back to his practice just as quick as he possibly could. He is an expert, but is giving up his time to this work and is sacrificing a great deal. Men of that class are found all through this department, so that there is not very much opportunity for the exercise of ordinary political patronage.

One of my difficulties is that I cannot quite understand the class of men the minister has in mind. Would the minister give us an illustration of the class of men he is employing and that he has to provide substitutes for when they leave? What class of men are they and what are they doing?

Take the medical men who are in charge of sanatoria and hospitals. They are medical practitioners and most of

them have served in the war. Many of them are back and are carrying on this work. But they know it is not going to be permanent and they are anxious to get back to their practice. That is one class. Then take the technical instructors who are established throughout the country. There is one in Ottawa, several in Toronto, and others in Winnipeg, Calgary and Vancouver. They possess technical qualifications and are carrying on technical education. The return men come in and are given a short course, according to the class of work they take. They are given, say, two or three months' instruction in these schools and the instructors would probably have five, six, seven, or eight departments in these various schools, handling anywhere from 100 to 200 men daily in those departments. The men who give that instruction are all technical men. Then, take the men who take charge of the industrial service. They go into all the industries in our largest cities and keep in touch with them all the time with a view to finding places for all returned men who are being temporarily trained. I would call a man of that class a highly technical man, as far as this work is concerned. Then we have men who follow up the returned men after they get positions and keep in touch with them. Once a man gets into an industry they go to see that man once a week. They keep in touch with the employer as well as with the man and see how the latter is getting along; they get a report from the man himself, and from his employer, or from the shopman. That work is going along all the time and there is a fairly large staff of men of that class. There is another staff of men called "aftercare" or "follow up" men. That is, after a man is trained, has completed his course, and is certified to, we have a certain type of man that follows the disabled soldier who has been retrained for a period of three, four, five months, or more, to make certain that he has been really established and that he has got back into civil life. The man who is looking after that work must have peculiar qualifications in order to carry out the duties that are cast upon him. I have forgotten how many employees there are but there are many hundreds in various parts of Canada carrying on this work. There is no doubt at all that these men know there is no future for them in that work, but they are making, as I say, real sacrifices in staying with it and assisting in the training and placing of these disabled men.	I
I am not going to complain any further, but I am more convinced than ever that these men are not at all a technical class.
They are not, in the ordinary sense.
The minister is speaking oif the man who is an employment agent.
No.

He is an employment agent, that is all he is. He looks around for places for the men who are trained in the vocational schools. He does not require to have* a previous, training of any kind; he is a man of good deportment, and good manners, and can talk civilly to people, and he goes around and looks for a position for some man whom he has in mind. He gets a position for him and he places him. Therefore, what is he but an employment agent? The man who has a little office in connection with some of the big industries of this country and who employs men on the spot is not a technical man by any possibility. He is a man who is necessary and must be a good man, but he is not in the ordinary sense a technical man. Technical men are
those who have received a high professional training or a scientific training of some kind. A special training of that kind is needed before one can he designated a technical man. The fellow who goes around to the boss of an industrial establishment and asks him how the returned soldier employee is doing cannot by any means be regarded as a technical man.

speechtext: Is not this a duplication of the powers that are now exercised by the Estates Branch of the Militia Department?

speechtext: Shall paragraph (d) carry?

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 41, to amend The Railway Act, 1919.
Explain,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The whole purpose of this Bill is to repeal subsection (c) of section 6 of the Railway Act as passed at the last session of the House. That section provides, in effect, that any railway which is controlled or operated by a railway which is under the legislative authority of Parliament, and any railway which controls or operates a railway which is under the legislative authority of Parliament, shall be under the legislative authority of Parliament, and all such railways are in general terms declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. It has been found by experience that the clause overshot the mark at which it was aimed, and that it has produced the result that in certain instances tramways running in cities have come within the wide terms of that article, and have consequently been declared to be work for the general advantage of 'Canada, with the result that the fixing of their fares becomes a matter for the Railway Commission, and they are withdrawn from the control of provincial utilities boards and so forth, and in a large measure from municipal control. A special instance that brought attention to this was the case of the British Columbia Electric Railway Company, which has been running a tramway in the cities of Vancouver and Victoria. The particular nature of the contract is not material, but the company does control and operate two very short roads, one of which was originally constructed by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the other under a Dominion charter. That state of facts brings the tramways under the legislative authority of this Parliament, and declares them to be works for the general advantage of Canada. There has been very strenuous objection on the part of the provincial authorities as well as on the part of the municipal authorities of these cities. I think it is fairly obvious that it is undesirable that by an omnibus clause of that kind we should get tramways running in particular cities declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada and subject to the control of the Railway Commission. Perhaps the wiser way, and probably even the only legal way, to make works which are purely local in their nature works for the general advantage of Canada, would be by specific declaration
TMr. A. K. Maclean.]
with regard to each work, although I do not want to commit myself absolutely on that proposition at the present time. This Bill is to repeal that section because it is considered that it was not contemplated to produce the results which it has produced. and which are open to serious objection.
Was the section referred [DOT] to a new one in the recent revision, or an old one?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It was a new one in
the revision of 1919. If my information is correct, what was principally in the mind of those who introduced it was the case of a regular steam railway in the province of Quebec which had come to be operated in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which it was considered highly desirable, and I think probably correctly so, to bring under the legislative authority of the Dominion and declared it to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. iBut, instead of proceeding by dealing with a particular railway, the method was taken of defining the whole class of railways as being for the general advantage of Canada, and subject to the legislative authority of Canada, with the result that in the net that was thrown out there were caught a good many fishes for which the fisherman was not looking at all.

The net for railways has been pretty broad.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (for the Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into committee on the following resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
That it is expedient to amend Section 477 ol the Canada Shipping Act, chapter 113 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, hy adding a provision that ships registered in Canada, employed in voyages between any port or ports in the province of British Columbia and the Port of San Francisco, or any port of the United States of America on the Pacific, north of San Francisco, shall he exempted from the payment of pilotage dues.

I desire to amend the resolution by inserting after the wtord "San Francisco" in the second last line, the following words, "and between any port in the province of British Columbia and any port in Alaska." The purpose of this amendment is to extend the privilege to vessels sailing between British Columbia and Alaska.
Will the minister explain the purpose of the resolution?

Its purpose is to extend to the province of British Columbia a privilege -which has for many years been accorded to the eastern provinces, namely, to exempt Canadian shipping -from pilotage within its own waters. Legislation of this nature in the first place was applicable to the Maritime Provinces and afterwards extended to Quebec.

I am not familiar with such a law affecting the harbour of North Sydney. I am not aware that a ship built in Nova Scotia and registered anywhere in Canada is exempt from pilotage dues, coming into the port of Halifax or any other port in that province. If there is such a law I am not at all familiar with it, but the minister mentions it as one reason for this proposed legislation. In the county of Cape Breton for many years there was a large fleet of steamers owned by the Dominion Coal Company, carrying coal from Sydney to Montreal. It was regarded as a hardship that every time they entered the harbour they should pay pilotage dues, and a regulation was passed whereby the Dominion Coal Company paid a lump sum annually and carried what was known as the " white flag ", by which pilots would know they were not to go out to the ship. That is the only regulation I ever heard of in connection with shipping in Nova Scotia in which any exemption was made. This seems to be largely a question affecting the pilotage authorities in British Columbia, but I think it would be desirable to know whether the pilots in that province have agreed to this legislation, Which no doubt, affects them materially. They are, no doubt, paid by dues.
No, they are paid by salary.
Still, it would be well to know if they are consenting to this.

The amendments proposed by the resolution originated from the report of a commission which was appointed some years ago to investigate certain matters of this nature in regard to which they made certain recommendations. In reference to the first point spoken of by my hon. friend, the Pilotage Act was passed in 1873 by which ships propelled wholly or in part by steam were exempt from payment of pilotage dues, if trading or employed on voyages beginning in any port in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick and
ending at the port of New York. Vessels engaged in that trade are exempt to-day. Later, vessels engaged in trading between Canadian ports and Newfoundland were exempted. Then, at another date, vessels trading between Quebec and any American port as far south as New York were exempted. The purpose of the present measure is to give to British Columbia the right to exempt from pilotage dues any Canadian registered vessels engaged in trade between +hat province and .points on the American Pacific coast as far as San Francisco. I am not aware of any opposition to the Bill from the pilots.

Are the motor boats that ply for trade subject to pilotage dues in British Columbia? I ask this question because I believe hon. members have been bombarded with letters from motor boat owners on the Pacific Coast complaining of a regulation that is being enforced there. The letters are couched in very strong language and.make certain charges against the inspectors of the department, and I wondered whether the pilotage dues formed the basis of their complaint. Why are those men being put out of business
Air. A. K. A1ACLEAN:	I really cannot
answer that question, but this Bill has no relation to the matter mentioned by the hon. gentleman. The gasolene boats are not subject to pilotage dues. I understand that the agitation in connection with the particular matter to which my hon. friend refers has relation to a regulation to insure safety in the operation of gasolene boats. Some one in British Columbia is a very strong and persistent correspondent on this subject, and every one in the House, so far as I know, has received a letter, although I do not recollect having received one myself.

The minister
says that he is not aware of any opposition from the pilots in regard to this legislation. During last session I called upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballan-tyne), accompanied by two of my friends, the hon. member for Belleohasse (Mr. Fournier) and the hon. member for L'Islet (Mr. Fafard), together with representatives of the Quebec and Montreal pilots.
I was not talking of all the pilots in the world. I was speaking of the pilots in British Columbia.

It was understood at the time, between the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and ourselves, that nothing

would be done in the matter at this session, but that the question would be taken up at the session of 1920. I fail to see why it should be taken up now. Why the rush? The navigation season is about over now.
Not in British Columbia. This merely refers to ships plying in Pacific coast waters as far south as San Francisco and as far north as Alaska. It has nothing to do with the Quebec pilotage district.

The understanding
with the Minister of Marine was that the pilots from all over the Dominion were to. send delegates or representatives to meet the minister and take up this question of pilotage, after which the minister would draw up a Bill to amend the Shipping Act. It seems to me it would he just as well to postpone this proposal and let the word of the Minister of Marine be respected. That was a fair understanding. He told me himself, sitting in his seat, that he would not do anything at this session, that it would only be done at the coming session. If he intends to hear representatives of the pilots from all over the Dominion, the Bill should not be taken up until he has heard them.

Referring to the British Columbia matter, while it is not exactly pertinent to the Bill, I may say that the charges contained in those letters were of a very serious character, reflecting on the officers of the Department of Marine to such an extent that anybody reading them must say that they were libellous. 'I think the Government should have an investigation to try and clear the department and see if there is anything wrong in the case of the inspectors, who are charged with having taken money for the purpose of putting some of these men out of business. I think the Government would be well advised to send some eastern man out there to straighten this matter out, because it is a great scandal on the coast and all over Canada.
Mr. A. Iv. MACLEAN: I shall direct the attention of the officers of the department to the remarks of the hon. gentleman.

We might perhaps show a little more care and scientific thought if we said "within Canadian waters," or "Canadian ports." This might -Cause some criticism or ridicule on the part of the authorities in'San Francisco and other American ports who might allege that this would be saying that a ship would not pay any 
pilotage anywhere on thhse voyages. We have no business to say that she shall not pay pilotage when going into the harbour of San Francisco.
That is not the intention.
Would it not be well to say "while in Canadian waters?"
Does the exemption apply only to foreign trade or does it apply, for example, to a vessel going from Vancouver to Prince Rupert? What would be the effect?
It would not apply.

Read it through carefully and see. I do not suppose that it is intended but the expression is: "between any port or ports in the province of British Columbia." Prince Rupert and Vancouver are both ports "within the province of British Columbia. I think the intention is to apply it to foreign trade only but it is capable "of another meaning.
Mr. A. Iv. MACLEAN: Do you mean that the words " or ports " should be struck out?
I am not suggesting what should be done; I am merely drawing attention to it.

As the resolution is drafted it would appear to me that the exemption from payment of the pilotage dues only applies to ships registered in Canada and on a voyage between any port or ports in the province of British Columbia and the port of San Francisco.
To foreign trade.

A ship may start at Prince Rupert, call at Vancouver and go on to San Francisco. That ship would not pay any pilotage dues. But I do not think it is quite clear that if the voyage ended at Vancouver the boat which started at Prince Rupert and came to Vancouver and stayed there would not be exempt from pilotage.

We do not intend to cover cases of that kind.

speechtext:
Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 36, to amend the Public Printing and Stationery Act. He said: This Bill has been prepared- by the Board of Civil Service Commissioners and is introduced at the instance of that board for the purpose of carrying into effect certain recommendations made by the committee which has examined into the working of the Printing Bureau and the Stationery Department of the Government. As the House is aware, a special committee was appointed some time ago to investigate that branch, and that committee has made an elaborate report containing some radical recommendations, one to reduce the staff by some 402 employees, which recommendation will be dealt with in an estimate to be submitted to the House, I believe, to-morrow. The other recommendation is in regard to the purchasing power now invested in the Printing Bureau and in the Stationery Branch. Under the present Act, which is chapter 80 of the Revised Statutes- of Canada, by section 19 there is authorized the appointment of a superintendent of printing, who is empowered:
-with the approval of the minister to purchase such material required for printing, electrotyping, stereotyping, lithographing and binding and other work of a like nature, -except paper.
Then by section 22 the appointment is authorized of a superintendent of stationery who:
-shall, under the direction of the minister, have charge of the purchase and supply of all printing and other paper and of all other articles of stationery required for the use of members and employees of the two Houses of Parliament and of the several departments of the Govern-men of Canada.
It seems that a system has grown up whereby another official in that department has been in the habit of making extensive purchases both of print paper and of other stationery. He holds the position of superintendent of outside printing. That position was never authorized by the Act, but it has been in existence for a number of years. Therefore there are really three purchasing branches in that department, and three officials with power to purchase; the superintendent of printing, the superintendent of stationery and the superintendent of outside printing. Under the recommenda-

tion of the reclassification committee it is proposed to appoint one officer who shall be known as superintendent of supplies.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: A new appointment?

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The position will be new and all purchasing power in that department will be vested in the Superintendent of Supplies. I am instructed by the Civil Service Commissioners that that does not involve any new appointment; it is merely a re-arrangement of the present offices and the duties pertaining thereto. The purchasing power now vested in the Superintendent of Printing, the Superintendent of Stationery and the Superintendent of Outside Printing will, when this Bill passes, be vested only in a Superintendent of Supplies.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What will become of the other two officials?

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
They have their duties
as described in this Bill and in the Act. They will be custodians of the supplies and will have the disposal of them, but the purchasing power is taken away from them.
The other clauses in the Bill are merely by way of amendment to the present Act in order that the provisions of this new Act may be made properly applicable. In the printing of the Bill two subsections were omitted which should be inserted. The Bill provides that section 24 shall be repealed. Section 24 should be re-enacted to provide for the introduction of the name of the new official that I have mentioned. In the committee stage I shall move to add two new subsections to 31A.
Motion (Mr. Guthrie) agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr Boivin in the Chair.
On section 3-Superintendent of Supplies to have charge of custody and supply of stationery.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
What becomes of this
Outside purchasing agent? Does he take this new position, or does he go out of office?

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: He continues in his position as Superintendent of Outside Printing, but he is deprived of any power of purchase.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the meaning of "Superintendent, of Outside Printing"? I understand it to have reference to the supervision of Government printing done outside the Bureau-in Winnipeg, for instance, or Halifax. Is that his work?

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes, that is the work he does now and will continue to do. But as I have said, he has been in the habit of making purchases. Under this Bill the purchasing power will be placed in the hands of a single official; the Superintendent of Stationery will lose any power to purchase which the former Act gave him, as will the Superintendent of Printing.

Section agreed to.
