Mr. GUTHRIE Section 24 of the present Act reads: "All purchases made by the Superintendent of Stationery." As the power to purchase has been taken away from the Superintendent of Stationery, section 24 should be re-enacted as section 30a, subsection 2, and in its new .form will read: "All purchases made by the Superintendent of Supplies."

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: At the last session we voted the money that the Government considered necessary to carry on the business of the Printing Bureau. This session we are to be asked to. vote 1276,000. In view of the proposed changes, the minister should make a full explanation of what is involved in this proposed expenditure.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The item that appears in the Estimates is for the reorganization of the Printing Bureau to carry out the recommendations of a special committee which made an investigation into the conditions prevailing in that department. The committee has reported that the services of 402 persons employed in the Bureau may be dispensed with and an annual saving of approximately half a million dollars, thus effected. The question arises what to do with the 402 employees. The scheme which the committee has reported involves an expenditure of $276,000, the amount which appears in the Estimates. The proposal is to superannuate these men for a period of five years. The employees are divided into several classes. Those who are under 45 years of age and who have worked in the Bureau for three years are entitled -I am speaking from memory-to a month's notice and a month's pay. Those between the ages of 45 and 55 are more liberally dealt with; and those between the ages of 55 and 65 more liberally still. Those over 65 who have been in the Bureau over ten years are entitled to a pension, equal, I believe, to half their wage or salary. To release these 402 employees involves the expend-

iture of the amount mentioned in the Estimates. Basing the figures on an actuarial table, the committee estimates that at the end of five years the total amount which the country will have had to pay is $276,000, the amount to be spent in the coming year being about $80,000. The saving effected will be half a million a year, and more when these payments cease. But this is a matter which can better be discussed when this item in the Estimates is taken up.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The scheme is not before us and we cannot really discuss it now, but when we reach it I am afraid the chief objection will be that we are going to create a -superannuation system for one branch of the Government service while neglecting all the other branches. With regard to the puchase of supplies, may I inquire whether it is contemplated that the Superintendent- of Supplies shall buy printing machinery?

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I should think it would include presses, electrotyping machinery, and the like. Section 24, which is to be re-enacted, sets forth in what way the purchases are to be made.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The section says:
"All materials and supplies required for printing, binding" and so on. I would say that that does not include machinery.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Presses and type would be required for printing.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes, but they are not supplies or materials required for printing. When you are dealing with an industrial exploitation you have the matter of machinery, supplies and materials to consider; each would be in a separate category.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Why not insert the
word "machinery" if that is the intention?

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I really cannot say
definitely whether the idea of the Commissioners was that this agent should have the power to buy machinery. I am advised by one of my colleagues that that was not their idea; I thought it was. However, I would rather not change the language of the Bill; it is just as it was drawn by the Commission.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-Superintendent of Supplies to purchase stationery, etc. and be responsible for outside work.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I move that the word
"one" in line twenty-one be struck out,

so that the sentence will read, "after section thirty thereof", and that "30A" be substituted for "31A" in line 22.
Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I move to add two subsections, 2 and 3, to 30A. Subsection 2 is a re-enactment of section 24 of the Act embodying the appropriate changes of language. It will read:
(2)	All purchases made by the Superintendent of .Supplies shall be so made upon requisition approved by the minister or as he directs, and, in the case of printing paper for parliamentary printing-, the Canada Gazette, and departmental reports, in accordance with contracts entered into with the like approval after tenders have been called for.
Subsection 3 will be:
(3)	All such purchases made on the authority of requisitions duly approved by the minister or as he directs shall be paid after audit by the accountant.
There has heretofore been no provision-for the auditing of the Printing Branch. While the Auditor General audited the Stationery Branch, he did not audit the Printing Branch, holding that he had no authority to do so. Subsection (3) is to provide that the Auditotr (General shall audit both the Printing Branch and the Stationery Branch.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The section my hon.
friend has read makes it clear that tenders must he called for in the matter of printing paper but in nothing else.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: YTes, that is it.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Is it wise to have
reform in the matter of printing paper, but go on in the old way with everything else?

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Printing paper is the
largest item. Other articles are purchased in very much smaller quantities and do not involve anything like the amount involved in the purchase of printing paper. There is also a general law in regard to purchases.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Then we do not need
this.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am informed it is only a departmental law.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is right in saying printing paper is a large item, but pretty nearly all items are large these days. Ink, for instance, is a large item. Suppose we take my hon. friend's -assumption is right, and that this covers machinery. The purchase of a new printing press might run into a very large sum of

money, higfier than the cost of printing paper. The purchase of type and type material and a lot of other things well known to those who are familiar with the newspaper business also involves a considerable expenditure. Printing paper is a large item, but there are several others, and I can see no reason for the system of tender and contract for printing paper and not for anything else.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Why not extend the
system of tender and contract to all supplies of the departments? Would that be embarrassing?

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think there should be some limitation. You would not ask for tenders, for instance, in a small purchase of lead pencils or mucilage.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I would suggest that
the minister advance the Bill as far as possible but leave it in committee, so that he may discuss the matter with his experts. Certainly I think there ought to be some limitation to buying other things than printing paper without tender and contract.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There is a regulation now in force, which affects all departments, requiring the minister's sanction where the purchase is in excess of $500. That may have been by Order in Council. Then in the case of public works in excess of $5,000 tenders, must be asked for. I do not know whether it refers to materials or not.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If there is a general rule covering everything there is no need for this provision, and if we are going to deal with printing paper we should deal with other items at the same time.

maintopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The minister will understand that as far as we on this side of the House are concerned our opinion is that the general rule should be tender and contract. Of course, we do not want tenders called for in case of a small purchase of lead pencils or anything of that sort.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

On motion of Hon. J. A. Calder (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) Bill No. 38, to amend the Immigration Act was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-free transportation of Immigration officers:
Has there been an explanation of this Bill? It might be called a deadhead Bill.

No, it is a live one. The explanation is this: Our immigration offcers board the trains crossing the border in order to see that the provisions of the Immigration Act are carried out. Under the law, if we chose we could stop every train at the border until that work was done, but by agreement with the railway companies our officers board the trains and travel for a certain distance in order to avoid delaying, the train. When our Immigration Act was amended last session, the section providing for the transportation of these officers was cut out, or it was cut out of the Railway Act. The result is that we must pay for the transportation of our officers when they travel on these trains, and that will mean a very great expense. If we do not provide for free transportation, the only thing left for us to do will be to stop the trains at the border.
Is the term "transportation" defined by the Railway Act or some other act?
It is defined in the Immigration Act.
It refers to railway transportation only?
I think it covers steamboats.
There might be some reason for this legislation in the case of trains crossing the boundary, but there is no limit to this. All immigration officers can deadhead all over Canada under this provision.
That is not the intention.

The intention of all statutes is gathered from the documents themselves, as my hon. friend's legal advisers will tell him. The course covered by this measure does not seem to me a very dignified proceeding. I think it is one of those things that might better be done by arrangement in a friendly way than by legal enactment, if the Minister says it is very important. We have gone a long way when we make the railway companies deadhead members of Parliament, and to make them deadhead a lot of our officials strikes me as not a very dignified proceeding.
The Act passed last session precludes any friendly arrangement.
Another case of defeating our own laws.

In the Railway Act last
session provision was made for free transportation to certain persons, and the section did not include immigration officers. This is intended to apply only to immigration officers who are working along the border and have to travel back and forth.

Could you not define
that in the Bill? The clause is very ugly as it is.

It reads, " in connection with their official duties."
Mr. MdMASTER: Though I suppose we could not ask a company to carry a Canadian citizen over an American railway line, still, as far as Highwater on the Boston and Maine, I imagine he could be carried free of charge. I agree with the hon. member, (Mr. Fielding), that it does not look well for us to state that, as a matter of law, transportation companies shall have the right to carry Canadian officials free of charge.

We might stipulate "in
connection with their official duties along the international boundary line."

Some such provision would do.
Mr. A. K. MA'CLEAN: What about entering ports?

The only places where
this is necessary are along our rivers where ferries run internationally and trains cross the border.
Mr. McMAS'TER: A man might get on at Highwater on the Boston and Maine and stay on perhaps until he reached Cowans-ville twenty or thirty miles further up the line, and your amendment would have to be sufficiently wide to cover the transportation.
Mr. CALDER. In the case of ships on the iSt. Lawrence, our officers very often go down stream a considerable distance. They used to get on at Rimouski and go to Quebec. On the Pacific coast, some of our officers go to Victoria and then cross to Vancouver. It seems to me that the matter would be a little difficult to cover. It is not the intention to apply this to inland travelling. So far as the other departments are concerned it has been eliminated. I do not think the railway companies should

be required to transport Government officials on Government business free of charge, and I can assure the hon. gentleman that that is not the intention in this case.
I accept the ministers's statement in regard to the intention, but a stranger reading our Act would consider this a strange provision.

In travelling on the
Grand Trunk would a Government official, say a Customs officer, have to pay Ms way between Montreal and Windsor, for instance, after the railway becomes our own?
Yes.
On our own railway? That is strange.
Is there anything to show that this applies to local border traffic?
I am not sure of that.
Do American officials who travel on our road on the border pay their fares?

They all have transportation, which is a great convenience to the railway companies. The American officers have the right to stop a train crossing the border, but instead of doing that an arrangement is made with the railway companies on both sides whereby the officers travel on the trains and do their business.
Mr. 'CURRIE: Do our officers travel on American trains?
Yes.

It is in the interests of the transportation companies that everything should be done to facilitate the work of the customs and immigration officers, and on that principle this provision is necessary.

I quite agree with that, but I had hoped that a friendly arrangement could be arrived at. The minister, however, says that owing to the strictness of the Railway Act of last year we practically prohibit such an arrangement. If that is the case I think he has to amend the present law.

Perhaps this provision
might be made: " Transportation companies shall furnish immigration officers such free transportation as may be required in connection with the examination by them of persons entering Canada."
I think it is better as it is.
This would apply to American officers coming to Canada on their official business?
Yes.

If in another Act there is a definite prohibition to the granting of free transportation to all persons except certain classes mentioned, should not you say in this Act: "Notwithstanding anything contained in "-such and such an Act?
This is the more recent legislation and overrides the other.

On that principle it is not necessary. But is it not expedient, in order to show that it is not a mere contradiction, but that in drafting this provision the legislature had clearly in mind a certain enactment in spite of what had been previously enacted?
If the committee desires it, that addition might be made.
On that point I would put myself in the hands of the Minister of Justice. .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The effect would be absolutely the same. By putting in " Notwithstanding " you would get the advantage of directing public attention to the fact that this Parliament knew what it was doing and wanted to tell every one that it knew what it was doing. But if you left it just as it is the legal effect would be absolutely the same, and perhaps the public would assume that we knew what we were doing when we did it, and were in effect repealing or modifying the provisions of a preceding law. I think there is more occasion for the " notwithstanding " when you are making some special provision that runs counter to some other provisions of the same Act with which you are concerned. But every provision of law that modifies pre-existing legislation takes effect, " notwithstanding."
Bill reported and read the third time and passed.

House again in committee on Bill No. 9 to amend the House ol Commons Act, and to provide that polling days at elections shall be public holidays-Mr. Jacobs-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This Bill has already been considered in committee as amended by the Select Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and as further amended by the committee of the whole House.



On section 1, paragraph 11a,-on vacancy occurring writ to issue within six months:
Could this Bill not be reprinted in its amended form?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The entire Bill as
amended may be found in Hansard, page 1433, unrevised edition.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If my memory serves
me, the Bill had been dealt with in its entirety by the committee but was held for consideration of the suggestion that paragraph 11a as amended by the Privileges and Elections Committee should be amended by striking out the words which limit the application of the clause to vacancies occurring by reason of the death of any member, or by reason of his accepting any office. Then the clause will be applicable in the case of a vacancy however occurring. We have considered that suggestion, but as the Bill is not a Government measure I do not desire myself to move the amendment. This is the Bill presented by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), who is presently represented, I understand, by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master). As far as the Government is concerned it is quite prepared to abide by the decision of the committee as to whether that amendment should or should not be made.

In the absence of the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) I would ask the committee to consent to this amendment mentioned by the Minister of Justice. It would appear to me to be wise that this provision, ordering a by-election to take place within a certain time, should operate no matter how the vacancy occurred. I would therefore move that the words " by reason of the death of any member or by reason of his accepting any office " should be stricken out.
Excepting any office under the Crown.

It says "any office." The clause would then read:
In the event of a vacancy occurring a writ shall he issued within six months after the receipt by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of the warrant for the issue of a new writ for the election of a member of the House of Commons.
No matter how the vacancy occurred the writ for the new election must be issued within six months after the vacancy occurs.
Is that quite clear?

I think so. It may be possibly necessary or advisable to put in after the words " in the event of a vacancy occurring " the words " in the membership of the House ". I would think that as we are amending the House of Commons Act, when we say " in the event of a vacancy occurring " it would be taken to mean that it was a vacancy in the membership of the House.	.
Six months after what?
Six months after the receipt by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of the warrant for the issue of a new writ.

It does not say six months after the vacancy occurs but it says six months after

?
After the receipt by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery-
Of what?

Of the warrant for the issue of a new writ. Just as soon as the member dies, or resigns, the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery issues his writ. But his writ is not acted upon until the Order in Council for the new election is passed by the Cabinet. As I understand it, the purport of the law as amended is that within six months after the issue of the warrant ordering a new election the issue of the writ shall take place.
It says nothing whatever about the issuing of.the warrant; it says within six months of the time that the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery receives something. What does he receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He gets the Speaker's warrant. I have sent for the Elections Act. This clause is to be inserted in the Elections Act, and I think if we had the Act here and read this as following immediately after what precedes it in the Election Act, it would become perfectly clear that the vacancy referred to is a vacancy in the membership of the House of Commons. We would also find there a provision as to the Speaker's issuing his warrant to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.

If the amendment is
worded properly and the six months dates from that, I can understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think it will be so
found, but I have sent for the Act to be certain. The last time I had it, it seemed to read clearly.

I am content if the
Minister says it is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not want to be
too positive but to me it seemed to be clear.

If it is dear that the
Speaker's warrant is referred to, that is all right.
M,r. CURRIE:	I would suggest that as
the whole Elections Act is to be revised within two or three months there is no use in cutting chunks out of it now and wasting the time of the House. As soon as the war is over the Wartime Elections Act expires and it is possible that within a few months the whole Elections Act will have to be overhauled and amended.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I might point out to
the hon. gentleman that we are not now dealing with the Elections Act or any amendments to it. What we are considering is an amendment to the House of Commons Act.
THE CHAIRMAN: Clause 2 of the Bill has been struck out entirely.
tMir. McMASTER:	I think paragraph 11
(b) has yet to be dealt with.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That was adopted
when the Bill was before the iCommittee on a previous occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We adopted it the
other evening. The Bill merely stood in Committee so that the point in doubt might be cleared up. I might perhaps say that if it should be found that the language is not perfectly clear, although my impression is that it is, I will see that such wording is made in the Bill in the Senate as will remove all doubt. But I will be surprised if my opinion is not correct on that subject.

Perhaps the Senate
may have a little hesitation in undertaking to amend the House of Commons Act, although the Upper House does remarkable things now.
Bill as amended reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When shall
the said Bill be read a third time?

If there is a possibility of changes in the wording of the Bill being made by the Law Officers of the House, I would suggest that the third reading go over to another day. It would certainly be irregular to make any changes in the Bill after it' has been read a third time.
121i

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I had understood that if changes were to be made they would be made in the Senate, but if the hon. member insists' the motion for the third reading must stand.

I think that will be preferable.
Mr. Mc'MASTER: May I address you on that point, Mr. Speaker. With all due modesty and deference I suggest that the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) is wrong if he maintains that the third reading cannot be had at the same sitting of the House at which a Bill has been discussed in Committee. It is true that such procedure is not usual, and it is discouraged by writers on constitutional and parliamentary law, but it is not, as a matter of fact, illegal or unconstitutional.

I have no desire to discuss the point at all, but what I am arguing is that we shall adhere to what has always been the custom of the House. The point I raise is this: If we permit the Law Officers of the House, or any other person, to make an amendment to a Bill after it has been read the third time, we are going to open the door to very many abuses. That is the only reason I have for holding the Bill up. That is .a bad practice to start here, and I do not-think the Government should permit-it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I must correct the hon. gentleman on one point. I did not suggest that the Law Officers, or anybody connected with this House should make any alterations in the Bill after the motion for the third reading had been adopted. What I did suggest was this: That if it should be found that the wording of the Bill is not perfectly clear, then in the Senate that wording should be placed beyond all doubt. That would not involve a change by the officers of the House. Furthermore, if the Senate did amend the Bill that amendment would have to come back here and we would then have an opportunity to consider it. The hon. gentleman, as I understand it, is within his right if he thinks there is any good purpose to be served by preventing the expediting of business to the extent proposed; but if he rests his case simply upon his apprehension that any alteration wouild be made in the Bill by any officer of the House, I might assure him that it is not contemplated at all and certainly will not be done.

With your permission,
Mr. Speaker, I would point out that the

proper procedure in respect of all House of Commons Bills is that they should be amended in this House. Before they are finally passed they are supposed- to be reviewed by the Law Officer of the House to see that the language is proper and that there is nothing of a wrongful character in the Bill. An officer is employed specially for that purpose and he reports on all these Bills. Of late years the practice has grown up of introducing Bills to correct some error in other Bills-1 think we have had one or two of that character this session. Now, I think it is well to adhere to the procedure that has prevailed for many years past, and that is for the Law Officer of the House to pass upon all Bills between the second and third reading and if any verbal errors are discovered they should be corrected. Our legislation should go to the Senate in proper form and not have the Upper House sending Bills back here in order to have verbal amendments made to them. That is my object in the .stand I am taking. I have no desire to hold up legislation, but I think my suggestion is a proper one and is in accord with the usages of this. House. If the minister is satisfied that the Bill is correct I am quite willing to let it go,, but the Senate is constantly making changes in our Bills on the ground that they are not worded in good English or that they contain errors, I therefore thought it right to make sure that this Bill was correctly worded and was in proper form before sending it to the Senate.

I believe it is a well
understood rule that unless very grave urgency exists the third reading of a Bill ought not to be proceeded with at the same sitting as the committee state. I think there is no great urgency in this matter. The world will wag on even if we have to wait for the third reading of this Bill until tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Even if there is no
urgency, some of us would 'like to wag away so soon as we conveniently might without any detriment to the public business. However, if the hon. gentleman insists upon his objection, I do not want to press the matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When shall the said Bill be read a third time?

At the next sitting of the House. Then the Minister of Justice can have a chance to look into the point which is in doubt.

On the motion of Hon. Mr. Doherty for the adjournment of the House:
May I ask what business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: All that now remains on the Order Paper are two Bills that are connected with prohibition. The Bills which were read a first time to-day will also be taken up to-morrow. They will be on the Order Paper for second reading. We have perhaps no assurance, but we would like to entertain the hope, that we will be able to dispose of all of these measures tenmorrow.
Then the Minister of Justice is really going on with the Temperance Bills to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think I can say we are really going on with those Bills tomorrow as we have always really intended they should be gone on with.
May we expect that the Grand Trunk Bill will be reprinted with amendments so that we will have them before us to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that the amendments will be printed in the Votes and Proceedings to-morrow. They will also appear in Hansard.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 11.26 p.m.
Saturday, November 8, 1919.
